coldRead.icp: Director of Nursing at a 25-bed rural Texas Critical Access Hospital who is also the scheduler, no IT department (one outside contractor), about to renew or sign a scheduling-software contract; reads once, start to finish

mondayActions: Pull the current scheduling software contract and look for response times, hours of coverage and a named contact
Start a support log: date, what broke, when reported, when fixed
Export a copy of the staff list and schedule history outside the system
Email the vendor: who is our named contact after go-live, and how do we reach them on a weekend?
Bring the six-row contract table to any demo or renewal call and ask for written answers
blockedActions: Write the actual contract clause for urgent response times: the post gives no sample wording to paste into a redline or renewal email
Judge whether a vendor's stated response time is good or bad: no benchmark numbers for urgent vs routine or for weekend coverage
Ask for a remedy if the vendor misses written response times (service credits, termination for cause without penalty, auto-renewal opt-out): the post says 'possibly to leave' with no mechanism
Ask for a data-return clause at contract end: no format (CSV/Excel), no timeframe, no scope (staff, schedule history, rules) beyond 'export at any time' tied to a billing dispute
Compare SimpleScheduleAI's response times to the table on this page: the times are only on /how-it-works

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
sections.notes: Clear. Fifth bullet points away to another guide before the post has started.

sections.heading: Why Can Scheduling Software Support Change After Go-Live?
sections.notes: L48-52 lands: implementation specialist moves on, Friday-evening schedule that will not post, nobody else to hand it to. This is my situation.

sections.heading: What Do Reviewers Say About Scheduling Software Support?
sections.notes: L56 tells me to look at review dates, then L60 leans on a January 2022 Deputy review. L58 quotes a medical-practice reviewer and then says it is not a hospital, so why lead with it? L62 brings in Aladtec, which I have never considered for nursing, and an acquisition I have not been told about yet; reread to work out why it is here. Interest drops in this section: it is about other vendors, not my contract.

sections.heading: Does an Acquisition Change Scheduling Software Support?
sections.notes: The heading asks about support. The answer is 'it can, hard to prove', and the only example (L68) is explicitly 'not a proven drop in support' but a product-direction change at a public-safety vendor. Then it sends me to another guide. I learned nothing I can use at renewal. Most likely skim point.

sections.heading: What Should a Scheduling Software Contract Say About Support?
sections.notes: The table is the reason I came. But 'A good answer looks like' gives no numbers (L77: 'Written times for an urgent problem' - is 4 hours good? 1 hour? next business day?). No sample clause wording. No remedy if they miss it (credits, right to terminate). L80 'during a billing dispute' is oddly narrow: I care about export at renewal and at exit. L81 'New customers still have the setup team' reread to get the point.

sections.heading: What Should You Do if Your Scheduling Software Support Has Already Declined?
sections.notes: Support log is practical. L89 'possibly to leave' with no how (notice period, termination for cause, auto-renew). L91 links to switching from Excel, but I would be switching vendor to vendor; reread to check I had not misunderstood.

sections.heading: How Does SimpleScheduleAI Handle Support?
sections.notes: Honest scorecard and the 'no reference customer' admission builds trust. But L100-101 answer 'response by urgency' and 'hours' with 'front of our queue' and 'see how it works', which is the exact 'We respond quickly is not a commitment' the table at L77 warned me about. L102 'one named contact': what happens when that person is sick or on leave?
